query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An Al/Ti-enriched high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a tailored composition (increased fraction of lightweight elements such as Al and Ti relative to heavier elements) will deliver a lower density while maintaining superior comprehensive mechanical performance (strength, ductility, and durability) compared to conventional HEAs or traditional light metal systems.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy alloy similar to the homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy with an established dual-phase FCC/BCC lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the alloy composition by increasing the overall fraction of lightweight elements (e.g., increasing Al and introducing or enriching Ti) in the high-entropy alloy formulation.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature and operational conditions typical for structural applications, without exposure to extreme environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces; retention of dual-phase (FCC/BCC) characteristics that facilitate synergistic deformation mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Substituting heavier alloying elements with lighter ones is expected to decrease the overall density while the engineered microstructure (as achieved via processing routes analogous to HPHT treatments) helps maintain or improve mechanical properties by promoting dislocation motion and mitigating interfacial stress concentrations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A material that exhibits a clear reduction in density (enhanced lightweight performance) with mechanical properties (strength, ductility, and durability) that are either on par with or superior to the baseline HEA composition.
generation.baseline: The standard Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy processed via homogenization, previously shown to have a dual-phase microstructure but not specifically optimized for lightweight performance.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated under ambient conditions and typical mechanical testing regimes; effects may vary if processing methods or service conditions differ significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of density reduction and retention of comprehensive mechanical performance is uncertain without experimental validation; trade-offs in manufacturability or cost may also arise.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline Al0.7CoCrFeNi composition and one with an adjusted composition featuring increased Al and added Ti. Process both sets under identical conditions (using homogenization and similar HPHT or equivalent thermal treatments). Perform systematic comparisons of their density and comprehensive mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility, and durability) under ambient conditions.
measurements: Measure the density using Archimedes’ principle or comparable techniques.
Perform tensile and compressive mechanical tests to assess strength and ductility.
Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., EBSD, SEM) to evaluate phase constitution and interface quality.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al/Ti-enriched alloy shows no statistically significant reduction in density compared to the baseline or if the comprehensive mechanical properties (strength, ductility, durability) drop by more than an acceptable margin (e.g., >10%) relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Various industrial and advanced functional applications require materials with high strength and ductility. Unfortunately, conventional processing strategies usually attain high material strength at the expense of deteriorated ductility [1] – [3] , whilst developing structures with substantial improvement of both strength and ductility is highly challenging. Recent successes in synthesizing superhard materials [4] – [6] have made the high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment [7] , [8] promising to achieve extreme properties in materials. The combination of pressure and temperature offers the great prospect for altering the microstructure of structural materials that would permit overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off. Given the vast space of control parameters involved in the HPHT treatment and the often complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures and temperatures [9] , [10] , it remains difficult to predict and interpret the mechanical behaviors of HPHT-treated structural materials, especially the abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics of non-equilibrium interfaces induced by the HPHT treatment [11] , [12] .

decision.trend: Early research on advanced alloys has progressively moved from conventional light metals and traditional composites—where trade‐offs in cost and overall performance were problematic—to the design of complex, high-entropy alloys with superior strength, ductility, and high-temperature or irradiation resistance. Many studies have focused on optimizing processing routes (e.g., high-pressure/high-temperature treatments, sputtering, laser powder bed fusion) and engineering microstructures to boost performance. However, these successes have mainly addressed performance under extreme or high-temperature environments, leaving the challenge of reducing density while maintaining comprehensive performance largely unaddressed.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge is to create a single material that is inherently lightweight yet delivers superior, well-rounded performance (mechanical strength, stiffness, durability, etc.) without incurring trade-offs in cost or manufacturability. In particular, integrating lightweight characteristics into a high-performance alloy remains elusive.
decision.lever: Adjust alloy composition by systematically incorporating a higher fraction of lightweight elements (for example, by developing an Al/Ti-enriched high-entropy alloy formulation)
decision.why: Given the trend of using compositional tuning in high-entropy alloys to tailor mechanical and functional properties, substituting heavier alloying elements with lighter ones is the most plausible route. This lever directly addresses the lightweight criterion while leveraging the established benefits of advanced alloy systems and their microstructural engineering to achieve a balanced, superior performance profile.
